description: How traditional and new media inform opinion and hold those in power to account.
content_html:
Why Does a Free Press Matter?

In a healthy democracy, citizens need accurate and independent information to make informed decisions: about who to vote for, which policies to support and how their institutions are performing. A free press — media organisations that are able to investigate and report without government interference — plays a central role in fulfilling this need. The media is sometimes called the “Fourth Estate”: alongside Parliament, the executive and the judiciary, it is seen as a pillar of democratic accountability. Without a free press, governments could act without scrutiny, corruption could go unreported and citizens would have less ability to hold power to account.

The Rights, Responsibilities and Roles of the Media

The media has a number of recognised rights. It has the right to report on matters of public interest: for example, investigating alleged corruption by a public official, reporting on the safety record of a large company, or uncovering evidence of wrongdoing in a public institution. The Human Rights Act 1998, which incorporates Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, protects freedom of expression — the legal underpinning of press freedom in the UK.

However, media freedom is not unlimited. Media organisations have responsibilities as well as rights. They are expected to be accurate: publishing false information that damages a person’s reputation without justification can constitute defamation. They are expected to respect personal privacy, especially where no public interest justifies an intrusion. The right of the media to report is balanced against individuals’ rights to a private life, protected under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Key Fact

The media has a right to investigate and report on public-interest matters, protected by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. It is also responsible for accuracy, respect for privacy and avoiding defamation. These rights and responsibilities must be balanced.

Traditional and New Media

Traditional media includes national and local newspapers, television news programmes (such as BBC News, ITV News, Channel 4 News) and radio. These outlets typically employ professional journalists who follow editorial codes and are subject to regulation. Television and radio broadcasters in the UK are legally required to be impartial — they must not take sides on controversial political issues. Newspapers are not subject to the same impartiality rules and can openly support political positions, though they are still subject to defamation law and press regulation.

New media includes social media platforms (such as Instagram, X, formerly Twitter, TikTok and Facebook), online news sites, podcasts, and personal blogs. New media has transformed political communication: politicians can now reach citizens directly, bypass traditional editorial gatekeepers, and respond to events in real time. Citizens can participate in political debates, share information and organise campaigns far more easily than in the age of print journalism. However, new media also creates challenges: disinformation — deliberately false content — can spread rapidly, and misinformation — inaccurate content shared without malicious intent — can be just as harmful.

Key Fact

Disinformation is false content deliberately created to deceive. Misinformation is inaccurate content spread without intent to deceive. Both can damage public trust and democratic debate, but their origins differ.

Press Regulation in the UK

Following widespread concern about journalistic practices — including phone hacking and the invasion of the privacy of victims of crime — a public inquiry led by Lord Justice Leveson reported in 2012. The Leveson Inquiry recommended a system of independent regulation of the press. This led to the creation of the Independent Press Standards Organisation (IPSO), which handles complaints about the print press, and a second body, IMPRESS. The regulatory system is voluntary for most print publications: major national newspapers are members of IPSO but not all press organisations are covered. Some critics argue the regulatory system does not go far enough; others argue that statutory (law-based) regulation of the press would itself threaten press freedom.

Supporters of stronger press regulation argue that voluntary systems allow newspapers to continue harmful practices with limited accountability. They point to the phone-hacking scandal, in which journalists at certain newspapers accessed the voicemails of private individuals — including crime victims and their families — without consent. They argue that statutory regulation, underpinned by law, with genuine sanctions for wrongdoing, is needed to protect ordinary people from intrusive or false reporting. They argue that a regulated press is not a silenced press: broadcasters are already subject to strict impartiality rules and this has not prevented good journalism.

Opponents of stronger statutory regulation argue that giving government the power to regulate what journalists can report is a fundamental threat to press freedom and democracy. They point out that authoritarian governments around the world use press regulation to silence critics and suppress inconvenient reporting. They argue that existing laws on defamation, privacy and contempt of court already provide adequate legal protection for individuals, and that a free press, however imperfect, is a crucial check on government power that must not be compromised by direct state control.

Censorship is the restriction of what can be published or broadcast. In the UK, there are lawful examples of restricted information: details that would prejudice a fair trial, information that would endanger national security, and material that incites hatred or violence. Courts can issue injunctions preventing the publication of certain information. These restrictions are narrow and must be justified under the Human Rights Act 1998. However, in other countries, censorship is used far more broadly to suppress political opposition, minority voices and independent journalism. For the GCSE specification, students should be able to describe examples of both justified and unjustified censorship and explain the tension between restricting information and protecting freedom of expression.

The Media’s Role in Informing and Influencing Public Opinion

The media does not simply report events; it also shapes how audiences think about them. The choice of which stories to cover, how to frame them, which voices to include and which to leave out all influence what the public considers important. Agenda-setting describes this power: if every major news outlet leads with the same story for a week, that issue will be at the top of public consciousness — even if other equally important issues are occurring simultaneously. The media also provides a forum for the exchange of ideas: interviews, debates, opinion columns, social media discussions and audience phone-ins all allow different viewpoints to be aired publicly. This function is especially important in the run-up to elections.
exam_tip_html: On an 8-mark “Discuss” question about the media, the most common error is focusing only on the benefits of a free press or only on the dangers of media power, rather than presenting both. Use connectives (“however,” “on the other hand”) to move between viewpoints. For a 12-mark “Evaluate,” name specific legislation or regulatory bodies — the Human Rights Act 1998 (Article 10), the Leveson Inquiry, IPSO — to lift into the Secure and Mastering bands. Your conclusion must make a substantiated judgement: state which consideration is most important and explain precisely why, rather than saying “it depends.” For source interpretation questions about media sources, remember to interpret what the source reveals — about bias, selectivity or agenda — rather than just summarising what it says.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A free press is essential to democracy: it informs citizens, provides a forum for ideas and holds those in power to account. Press freedom is protected by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights via the Human Rights Act 1998.
  • Traditional media (newspapers, TV, radio) and new media (social media, online news, podcasts) each have distinct roles; new media has democratised communication but also increased the spread of disinformation and misinformation.
  • Press regulation in the UK is largely voluntary; the debate over whether stronger statutory regulation is needed involves a genuine tension between protecting individuals from harmful journalism and protecting press freedom from government interference.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following bodies handles complaints about the print press in the UK?
A) Ofcom
B) IPSO
C) The Supreme Court
D) The BBC Editorial Standards Committee
State what is meant by the term 'freedom of expression'.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks. 1 mark for a basic statement (e.g. 'the right to say or publish what you think'). 2 marks for a developed statement that captures the legal dimension (e.g. 'the right to express opinions and publish information, protected in the UK by Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights via the Human Rights Act 1998, though subject to lawful restrictions such as defamation law and protection of national security').

practice_questions.text: Explain why accurate reporting by the media is important in a democratic society.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. A single fully developed point with cause and consequence can score 3-4 marks.

Acceptable points include:
- Accurate reporting allows citizens to make informed voting decisions (point); if the media publishes false information about candidates or policies, voters may make choices based on misleading premises, undermining democratic legitimacy (consequence).
- A free press that reports accurately can expose wrongdoing by those in power (point); without accurate investigative journalism, corruption and abuse of power are harder to detect and challenge (consequence).
- Inaccurate reporting can damage individuals' reputations unfairly (point); this is why defamation law exists — to balance press freedom with protection for individuals (development).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional media research organisation published a 2024 briefing: "A survey of 1,800 adults found that 54% said they trusted traditional broadcast news (TV and radio) as their main source of political information. Only 22% said they trusted social media as their primary source for political news. However, 61% of 18-24 year olds said they had shared a news story on social media without checking if it was accurate first."

What does the extract suggest about the challenges of new media in a democratic society? Use the extract and your own knowledge in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for accurately identifying what the source shows (traditional media is more trusted but social media is widely used, especially by young people, without accuracy checks); 1 mark for interpreting the significance (social media spreads news rapidly but accuracy is not verified, creating risk of misinformation and disinformation circulating widely); 1 mark for using own knowledge to develop the point (e.g. distinguishing misinformation from disinformation; referencing the role of IPSO in regulating print but the absence of equivalent regulation for social media; or the Leveson Inquiry's concerns about press practices); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement (e.g. the source suggests that while new media increases participation and speed of information, the lack of editorial gatekeeping creates democratic risks that current regulatory frameworks may not adequately address).

practice_questions.text:
A group of journalists is campaigning against new proposed laws that would require online news platforms to register with a government regulator.

Discuss whether governments should have more powers to regulate online media and social media platforms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced two-sided discussion using connectives. Arguments for greater government regulation might include: unchecked spread of disinformation can undermine democratic elections; social media platforms have been slow to remove harmful or false content; traditional broadcasters are already regulated without destroying press freedom. Arguments against might include: government regulation of online speech risks censorship and chilling free expression; authoritarian governments routinely use such powers to silence political opposition; existing defamation law and platform terms of service already provide some protection. Names at least one specific law or body (Human Rights Act 1998, IPSO, Article 10 ECHR). Reaches a substantiated position.

Secure (5-6 marks): Both perspectives present, broadly accurate, at least one named reference. Connectives used.

Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points on at least one side; limited development; no named example.

Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic statements; largely descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
A national newspaper editorial argues: 'A free press is the most important safeguard of democracy in the UK.'

Evaluate whether a free press is the most important safeguard of democracy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10-12 marks): Full two-sided argument. Arguments for the free press as the most important safeguard might include: the Leveson Inquiry highlighted how the press uncovered the phone-hacking scandal; investigative journalism has exposed MPs' expenses fraud, corporate corruption and public safety failures; freedom of expression (Article 10, Human Rights Act 1998) is foundational to public debate. Arguments for other safeguards being equally or more important might include: free and fair elections, an independent judiciary (free from political interference), the rule of law, the Human Rights Act 1998 as a framework protecting all rights, or parliamentary scrutiny of the executive — all protect democracy even when the press fails. Substantiated conclusion weighs which is most important and explains why, with reference to named examples.

Secure (7-9 marks): Both sides present, at least one named institution or legislation per side. Conclusion present.

Developing (4-6 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or underdeveloped. Some real-world reference. Conclusion thin or absent.

Emerging (1-3 marks): Basic statements. No substantiated judgement.

flashcard_questions.a: Yes — broadcasters must be impartial; newspapers do not face the same legal requirement.
Established news outlets such as national newspapers, TV news and radio journalism.

glossary_terms.definition: The principle that journalists and news organisations can report on matters of public interest without prior government approval or censorship.
Information about events or issues that it is in the general public's interest to know about, even if those involved would prefer it to remain private.
The publication of a false statement that damages a person's reputation; written defamation is called libel, spoken defamation is called slander.
Established news outlets such as national and local newspapers, television news broadcasts, and radio journalism.
Digital platforms and online services that allow users to create, share and interact with content, including social media, blogs, podcasts and online news sites.
False information that is created and spread deliberately to mislead people.
False or inaccurate information spread without necessarily intending to deceive.
The suppression of speech, public communication or information that may be considered harmful, sensitive or politically inconvenient.
The theory that media organisations significantly influence what issues the public considers important by choosing which stories to cover and how prominently to feature them.

items.title: More or Less — BBC Radio 4
items.description: Tim Harford's programme debunks misleading statistics in news stories — a masterclass in spotting the gap between how the media presents data and what it actually means.

items.title: Newscast — BBC Sounds
items.description: The BBC's own news podcast — a useful case study in how impartial broadcast journalism works in practice, with stories covered from multiple angles.

items.title: How to Spot a Misleading Graph — TED-Ed
items.description: Teaches you to recognise when data visualisation in news coverage is designed to mislead — a practical media literacy tool.

items.title: You Would Be a Terrible Leader — CGP Grey
items.description: Explains why accountable, democratic systems require independent scrutiny — makes the case for why a free press acts as a check on power.

items.title: Spotlight (2015)
items.description: The true story of the Boston Globe's investigative journalism that exposed institutional wrongdoing — a gripping case study of investigative journalism serving the public interest.

items.title: The Post (2017)
items.description: The Washington Post's decision to publish the Pentagon Papers despite government opposition — shows the tension between press freedom and state power in action.

items.title: Good Night, and Good Luck (2005)
items.description: Edward Murrow's use of TV journalism to challenge McCarthyism — a landmark case study of the media holding government to account, with lessons for today's debates on press freedom.

items.title: Full Fact — Independent Fact Checking
items.description: The UK's leading independent fact-checker — find out how to verify claims made in news coverage and understand how fact-checking organisations work.

items.title: IPSO — The Editors' Code of Practice
items.description: The code that governs standards for UK print journalism — understand what responsibilities newspapers have under self-regulation and how IPSO handles complaints.
